fidelity: Based on the provided Bradley-Terry-Davison (BTD) probabilistic model results, the optimal sequence for removing multiple image degradations is highly dependent on the nature of the degradations. Here are the key insights and actionable recommendations for multi-degradation image restoration pipelines (optimized for image fidelity): 1. Key Insights into Degradation Removal Order. A. JPEG Compression Artifacts Must Be Removed First: When an image suffers from JPEG compression alongside other degradations (like noise or blur), removing the JPEG artifacts first is overwhelmingly the best choice. vs. Defocus Blur: JPEG removal -> defocus deblurring wins 81% of the time. vs. Noise: JPEG removal -> denoising wins 82% of the time. Why: JPEG compression creates blocky, structural artifacts. If you attempt to denoise or deblur an image first, the models will treat these blocks as underlying image structures, amplifying or solidifying the artifacts. B. Rain (Structured Occlusions) Should Be Removed Before Global/Spatial Changes: Rain streaks act as foreground occlusions. They must be removed before attempting to alter the image's resolution or global atmospheric conditions. vs. Haze: Deraining -> dehazing wins 69% of the time. (Haze estimation relies on atmospheric light; rain streaks disrupt this estimation). vs. Low Resolution: Deraining -> super-resolution wins 56% of the time. (Super-resolving first would upscale and distort the rain streaks, making them harder for the deraining model to recognize and remove). C. The Order for "Darkness" (Low Illumination) depends on the Secondary Degradation: There is no "one-size-fits-all" rule for brightening; it depends entirely on what else is wrong with the image: Dark + Noise: Brighten first, then denoise (wins 52% of the time). Brightening amplifies noise. It is better to amplify the hidden noise first so the denoising model can "see" and remove the full extent of it, rather than denoising first and leaving hidden noise to be exposed later. Dark + Motion Blur: Deblur first, then brighten (wins 42% of the time, with a high tie rate of 42%). Brightening a blurred image might alter the light trails and blur kernels, making it harder for the deblurring network to track motion trajectories. D. Super-Resolution Should Precede Motion Deblurring: Low Res + Motion Blur: Super-resolution -> motion deblurring wins 80% of the time. Why: Deblurring networks rely heavily on fine structural details to estimate motion kernels. Upscaling the image first gives the deblurring model more pixels and spatial context to work with. E. Defocus Blur is Addressed Before Atmospheric Global Changes: Defocus Blur + Haze: Defocus deblurring -> dehazing wins 70% of the time. Why: Defocus blur alters object edges and depth perception. Correcting the focal structure of the image first allows the dehazing model to better estimate transmission maps (depth) to remove the haze. 2. General Recommendations for Restoration Pipelines: If building a cascaded, multi-step image restoration pipeline based on these probabilities, the operations should roughly follow this hierarchy from first to last: Digital/Encoding Artifacts (Highest Priority): Always run JPEG compression removal first. It has the highest win-loss disparity in the dataset. Foreground/Structured Occlusions: Perform Deraining next to uncover the true underlying scene. Spatial Up-sampling: Perform Super-Resolution before tackling motion blur, to give subsequent models sufficient pixel density. Structural Integrity (Blur): Perform Deblurring (both defocus and motion) before applying global lighting or atmospheric changes. Global/Atmospheric Corrections: Perform Dehazing or Brightening toward the end of the pipeline (with the caveat that brightening must occur before denoising). Denoising (Lowest Priority): Denoising should generally happen last, particularly after tasks like JPEG removal or brightening, which can alter the noise profile.
perception: Based on the provided Bradley-Terry-Davison (BTD) probabilistic model results, here are the key insights and actionable recommendations for multi-degradation image restoration pipelines, specifically optimized for human perception. 1. Strongly Dictated Orderings (Critical Priorities): When perceptual quality is the goal, certain degradations strongly demand a specific processing order. Reversing these orders leads to significantly degraded results. Remove Weather before Upscaling (85% Preference): For low resolution + rain, deraining must precede super-resolution. Upscaling a rained-on image likely amplifies the rain streaks, making them much harder to remove later. Fix Defocus Blur before Haze (74% Preference): For defocus blur + haze, defocus deblurring must precede dehazing. Dehazing relies on contrast and atmospheric light estimation, which is likely skewed if the image is out of focus. Remove Compression Artifacts before Deblurring (68% Preference): For defocus blur + JPEG artifacts, JPEG compression removal must precede defocus deblurring. Attempting to deblur an image with JPEG blocking artifacts will likely amplify the blocky structures. 2. Moderately Preferred Orderings (General Best Practices): These pairings show a clear, though less extreme, perceptual preference. Global Illumination before Denoising (54% Preference): For dark + noise, brightening should precede denoising. While brightening an image amplifies noise, modern denoisers (like xrestormer) appear better equipped to handle well-lit noise than brightening algorithms are at handling post-denoised dark images. Remove Compression before Denoising (50% Preference): For JPEG artifacts + noise, JPEG artifact removal should precede denoising. Similar to deblurring, denoising networks may struggle to distinguish between sensor noise and JPEG blocking, making it safer to remove macroblocks first. 3. Order-Agnostic / Flexible Pairings (Low Impact): In these scenarios, the BTD probabilities show high tie rates or nearly even win/loss ratios, indicating that processing order has a marginal impact on human perception. Dark + Motion Blur: Brightening first (44%) vs. Motion deblurring first (42%). Haze + Rain: Dehazing first (40%) vs. Deraining first (38%). Both are atmospheric degradations, and the order of removal is perceptually interchangeable. Low Resolution + Motion Blur: Super-resolution first (38%) vs. Motion deblurring first (32%, with a 30% tie rate). Phase 3: Fine-Grained Polish & Upscaling (Do this last). 5. Dehazing / Denoising: Handle atmospheric scattering and sensor noise after the structure, lighting, and focus are established. 6.
